The Chimpanzee mathematics is a probabilistic system. Probabilistic means it works with chances: it says how likely a thing is, instead of pretending to know for sure. The system is built from the chimpanzee's own body, its own behaviour, and its own evolutionary history, going back to the human-chimpanzee common ancestor, about 6 to 7 million years ago. It measures the chimpanzee itself, it measures the animals it evolved from, and it measures the lesser animals that share its forest. Every measurement is written in plain words first, then in numbers, so the record can be read by a person, by another animal system, and by the Signature translation.

The framework covers measurement, geometry, statistics, and probability. Measurement means giving a size or a count a number and a unit. Geometry means describing shapes, such as the shape of a home range or the shape of a body. Statistics means counting many examples and finding the middle and the spread. Probability means the chance that something happens. Together these let the chimpanzee's mathematics describe what the chimpanzee is, what it does, and what is likely to happen next.

The system is complete in this sense: nothing in it needs a human unit to work. The chimpanzee is measured in its own units, made from lesser animals. Human units are kept only as a translation, so people can read the same numbers in kilograms and metres. The chimpanzee's own mathematics stands on its own. Body mass is not one fixed number. It is a range, because young animals are smaller, old animals vary, and food seasons change the body. The record therefore gives a range and a middle value, not a single pretend-exact number. That is what probabilistic measurement means here: the range is the fact, and the middle is the best single summary of it. The same rule holds for height, arm reach, and every other body measurement in this system.

Self-measurement is the heart of the program: the animal must be measurable in its own system. From it the system builds larger units by counting: ten galago (bushbaby) units, one hundred galago (bushbaby) units, and one thousand galago (bushbaby) units. Every unit is named in plain words, and every unit is tied to a real animal that is smaller than the chimpanzee, so the units are lesser-animal units in the true sense.

Length is measured the same way, with a lesser animal's body as the ruler: the length of a {lesser} is the small length unit, and the {animal}'s own arm span and stride are counted in those small lengths. Time is measured in plain counts of days and seasons, because the forest gives the {animal} days and seasons, not clocks. Counting is the common root: mass, length, and time are all counts, and counts can be translated into human kilograms, metres, and days without changing what was counted.

Why lesser animals? Because the order says each animal's math must be able to measure any lesser animal, and the animal itself must be measurable in its own system. Units made from lesser animals satisfy both rules at once: the lesser animal is measured by its own body, and the {animal} is measured by counting those bodies. No unit in this system is invented from nothing; every unit names the animal it comes from.

Probability is the chance that something happens. This record gives a probabilistic model of a chimpanzee behaviour: the chance that a chimpanzee in a fission-fusion community that splits into small parties and gathers again moves to a new feeding place on a given day. The model does not claim a fixed answer. It gives a chance, and it says what the chance depends on: the season, the fruit in the trees, and the size of the group. When fruit is plentiful, the chance of moving is low; when fruit is scarce, the chance of moving is high. That is a model: a simple rule that says what is likely, and why.

The numbers in the model are ranges, not promises. A range such as 'about 3 times in 10 days' means that in ten similar days the move happened about three times. If new observations change the count, the range changes too. That is how the system stays honest: the probability is always tied to counted examples, and the count is written in the record. Where no count exists, the record says the chance is unknown, and the model is marked as a design estimate, not a measured fact.

The same probabilistic method is used for every behaviour in the {animal} system: feeding, resting, travelling, calling, and sleeping. Each behaviour gets a chance, a range, and the conditions that raise or lower it. The mathematics is therefore not a list of certainties; it is a working map of what is likely, built to be corrected by better counts.

The sleeping place is a point in that shape, and the feeding trees are points too. Geometry turns the {animal}'s life into shapes that can be drawn, measured, and compared: this year's range against last year's, one troop's range against another's, the {animal}'s range against a lesser animal's range.

All shapes are drawn from real behaviour: the chimpanzee lives in the forests of West and Central Africa, eats fruit, leaves, insects, and sometimes meat, and moves in a fission-fusion community that splits into small parties and gathers again. The geometry follows the life, not the other way round. Where the exact size of a range is not published, the record says so and gives the shape without inventing its size.

The date is a range from the science, not a single year, because the science reads it from fossils and from DNA clocks, and both methods carry uncertainty.

Its closest living relatives are the other great apes. The {animal} shares the most recent common ancestor with its sister species, and a more distant common ancestor with the rest of the family. The record lists the relatives in order of closeness, with the shared ancestor named for each step. Where the science disagrees about a date or a branch, the record says the science disagrees, and keeps both readings rather than choosing one in secret.

Evolutionary mathematics cascades through these relationships: a measurement made for the {animal} can be compared with the same measurement for a relative, and the difference can be counted. That comparison is a mathematical relationship, and it is how the {animal}'s system connects to the other animal systems without losing its own identity.

Each number is placed beside the same number for the gorilla, the chimpanzee, the orangutan, and the bonobo, so the differences can be seen at a glance, and the similarities too.

Comparison is not ranking. A bigger animal is not a higher animal, and a smaller animal is not a lower one.
